en: One Scroll of the Ritual for the Contemplative Practice and Recitation of the Bodhisattva Cultivating the Prajñāpāramitā.
Compiled by the Grand Master of the Household, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Duke of Sui, [Name].
I take refuge in the Mother Prajñā, the pure and wondrous Dharmakāya.
Now, relying upon yoga, I shall expound the methods of contemplative practice:
Directing the mind throughout the entire Dharma-realm, across the ocean of all Buddha-fields.
Visualize your body surrounded; through this, you shall attain liberation.
Visualize your body surrounding all the Buddhas, with each Buddha surrounded by a host of bodhisattvas holding exquisite offerings.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, As well as the assembly of great Bodhisattvas,
Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas— The entire treasury of the True Dharma,
without exception, One should contemplate it all as pervading one's own body.
All [beings] before the assembly appear as clearly as if facing them eye-to-eye;
all arise from the pure mind. Performing vast and manifold offerings, one makes immeasurable offerings and pays homage continuously and without interval.
With palaces, exquisite fly-whisks, and canopies, with countless multitudes of towers,
pavilions, flower garlands, powdered incense, and ointments, adorned with various jewels—
may all these ritual offerings fill the entire realm of space.
With a mind of earnest devotion, I offer these to all the Tathāgatas;
as the buddha-fields are like space, so too are the Buddhas,
and so too are the Buddha-dharmas— just as the offering to the Dharma is.
Having known that all are immeasurable and that there are boundless lands in the ten directions, he spoke these words: "I pay homage to all Tathāgatas.
The mantra for paying universal homage to all Tathāgatas is as follows:
Various and supreme, immeasurable dhāraṇīs spoken in the Mahāyāna sūtras are the heart of the Buddha;
one should recite them with earnest diligence,
give rise to pure faith, and focus single-mindedly on a single object.
For the sake of all sentient beings, having observed supreme enlightenment,
one should immediately bared the right shoulder, place the right knee upon the ground,
and stand with palms joined in sincerity, speaking these words:
Whether committed by myself, caused to be committed by others, or rejoiced in by myself or others—
through the transgressions of body, speech, and mind—
I pray that all Buddhas will take pity on me for the ten million offenses committed in this life, and even those from beginningless time.
And when I sit upon the seat of enlightenment, may I never again commit such transgressions;
through this supreme confession, by means of true observation,
may the fire of the Buddha’s vow-knowledge incinerate all [faults] until nothing remains.
The grasper and the grasped— all are but mind alone.
The Buddha-fields and the offerings, the grasper and the grasped— the Bodhisattva,
dwelling in meditative equipoise, sees the mind as being like a reflection.
One who can apprehend conceptualizations through the signless abides in emptiness;
the characteristics of both existence and non-existence are absent. This is called the characteristic of emptiness:
it is neither non-existent nor existent, for it is not separate from the single nature.
The object, the subject, and the act of offering—these three are free from conceptual construction because they are non-conceptual;
thus, this offering is supreme. Such is the supreme offering, as well as the practice of circumambulation.
All heavy sins and transgressions are extinguished without remainder;
Knowing the nature of greed to be non-greedy, one immediately enters the emptiness of the nature of greed;
Knowing the nature of hatred to be non-hatred, one immediately enters the emptiness of the nature of hatred.
Knowing that the nature of delusion is itself without delusion, one thus enters the emptiness of the nature of delusion.
Observing the principle of the true reality of all afflictions in this way,
those who possess such wisdom, by means of emptiness, are without conceptual discrimination.
Just as a lotus dwells in water yet remains unstained by it,
so should the practitioner contemplate;
having thus purified body and mind, one should then form the samaya-mudrā.
With the two hands joined together, one should place them upon the heart and visualize the Buddha throughout the void; recite the mantra three times.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vajra-jali. Next, form the vajra-bond: interlace the ten fingers with their backs facing outward;
this forms the seal of the secret bond.
The Vajrabandha Mantra.
The mantra is as follows:
As before, with the vajra-bind, strike it upon the heart.
One who can extinguish all fetters and afflictions and reveal the palace of liberation should then recite the Heart-Mantra for Opening the Mind, as follows.
Next, form the Seal of Arising Wisdom (*utpāda-jñāna-mudrā*), as before with the Vajra-bond (*vajra-bandha*).
Samādhi and Prajñā enter the palms. To summon [the wisdom] of perfect nirvāṇa and to summon the wisdom of all modes (sarvajñatā), the mantra is recited.
Next, bind the vajra-fist, placing the forefinger and the middle finger upon the ring finger and the little finger.
The vajra body, speech, and mind are closely united and immovable.
Recite the Vajramuṣṭi mantra while forming the samaya mudrā;
thus one spontaneously becomes Samantabhadra.
Having completed the binding, extend the earth-touching and wish-fulfilling mudrās;
with the body situated within the moon disc, recite the Samaya-mantra.
Next, perform the Great Truth-vow mudrā by crossing the earth-touching and wish-fulfilling fingers into a bind.
With generosity, wisdom, meditative concentration, and knowledge held upright;

with the two fingers [of the hands] and the three touches, one plants the seeds of weary detachment within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Being able to eliminate [afflictions] and increase compassion, one should further recite the mantra as follows:
Next, one should perform the ritual for warding off obstacles:
form the two vajra-fists with the hands of the Vajrayakṣa;
bend the thumbs and ring fingers and place them at the mouth and both cheeks; then visualize one’s own body as being identical to that Honored One.
Recite the mantra with a stern voice while glancing to the left and right.
The mantra of the Vajrayakṣa is as follows:
"May all obstructors be utterly dispersed in the four directions."
Second, visualize the syllable MAṬA; it revolves like the orbs of the sun and moon.
With the Vajra-fists of śamatha and vipaśyanā, place them respectively upon the two shoulders.
Following the movement of the sun, perform a circular gaze to encompass the realms of the ten directions.
Recite the Vajranetra mantra as follows:
One should enter samādhi; form the mudrā as before and place it facing upward upon the crossed legs; keep the body perfectly upright.
Closing his eyes, he entered right concentration and beheld throughout the entirety of space Buddhas as numerous as sesame seeds;
because all those Tathāgatas recalled their former vows, they spoke with one voice in different mouths.
The Professor recites the mantra, focusing single-mindedly on the principle of the true nature of reality.
Reciting this mantra repeatedly, one settles the mind within and observes;
gradually, this extends throughout the entire dharma-realm.
The characteristic of all space is that space itself is without characteristic;
through the yoga of space, it pervades the ten directions once the practitioner has entered.
The samādhi of the profound essential nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* realizes,
within the state of true reality, a great lunar disc equal in extent to the *dharmadhātu*,
its radiance universally illuminating all with tranquil coolness.
Arousing great compassion for all sentient beings who are scorched by the fires of the three realms,
he regards them as his only child and gives rise to a profound desire to rescue them,
thinking: "What shall I do now?"
He causes those who have not yet attained deliverance to attain deliverance;
he causes those who are not yet liberated to attain liberation;
and he causes those who have not yet found consolation to find consolation.
Causing those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa to attain it,
one then enters the samādhi of the yoga of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity),
visualizing one's own body as the Mother Prajñāpāramitā.
Wearing a crown of five Buddhas and celestial garments and necklaces,
golden light radiates from every pore,
flowing forth as immeasurable Buddhas.
Again, he forms this thought:
"My body and the Bodhisattva Prajñāpāramitā are non-dual and without distinction.
He then empowers the four places [of his body] with the vajra-protection of the Bodhisattva.
Form the two-vajra-bind with the thumbs and index fingers extended like needles;
place the mudrā at the heart, the brow, the throat, and the crown.
Having accomplished the yoga of the deity, recite the mantra as follows:
Next, bind the crown of the five Buddhas:
with both hands in the vajra-bond, the thumbs and ring fingers are shaped like a sword;
place the forefingers upon the middle joints at the crown of the head, then [extend them] toward the four directions; finally, circle the two fists in front of the forehead.
Like a crest-jewel tied at the back of a garland, hanging down with the appearance of a sash.
The mantra for the jeweled crown of all Tathāgatas is:
Oṃ Bukk. Next, recite the mantra of the Vajra Family:
Vajrasattva. Next, recite the mantra of the Ratna family:
Vajraratna. Next, recite the mantra of the Padma family:
Vajradharma. Next, recite the mantra of the Karma-kula:
Vajrakarma. Next, recite the empowerment mantra of the Vajramālā:
Oṃ vajramālāviśodhaya hūṃ svāhā. Next, perform the armor mudrā:
form the two hands into the vajra mudrā.
Clasping the armor for oneself and others,
with the index fingers entwined,
one always achieves great protection.
Then, recite the Armor Mantra:
Oṃ vajrakavaca vajriṇi kuru vajra haṃ. With this armor mudrā and by reciting the mantra, one dons the armor.
One immediately attains a body of vajra-nature and acquires vajra-longevity; for as long as one lives,
one receives great empowerment and protection.
It cannot be thwarted or destroyed in any circumstance;
having donned the armor,
they strike their palms together to inspire joy.
Next, recite the Vajra-Ānanda mantra as follows:
"By means of this heart-mantra, one is released from bondage and attains joy;
one obtains the vajra-body, just like Vajrasattva."
Having entered the vajra everywhere, one should form the great mudrā before the body according to the ritual rules. Contemplating the Great Sattva,
one should visualize that Wisdom Sattva within one's own body.
To summon, lead in, bind, and cause [the deity] to rejoice, thereby effecting accomplishment, one should recite the *Prajñāpāramitā* Universal Entry Mantra as follows:
Oṃ dharmavajra aḥ. Next, one should recite the *Prajñāpāramitā* Contemplation of the Heart Mantra as follows:

Oṃ dharmavajre ānaya hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ. This is the great *mahāsattva* mantra for summoning, entering, binding, and gladdening the mind. Reciting the *samaya-satvaṃ*, it enters everywhere from behind as a moon disc.
Within that, one should visualize the *sattva* at the rear:
"I am the *samayasattva*, *sattvaṃ* [together with the preceding syllables], following that mudrā.
Thus one should practice the visualization of oneself as that *sattva*.
The adamantine speech having been accomplished,
one is able to achieve all mudrās.
The practitioner then, within the maṇḍala before the image of the central deity, [proceeds].
Visualize a pavilion of the seven precious gems with four gates opened;
within that palace, contemplate the gateway of the letter *bhūḥ*,
which constitutes the Mother of Prajñāpāramitā.
They are surrounded by the ten pāramitās,
as well as the eight offerings, the four gate-hooks and locks, and the celestial hosts of the eight directions;
all are visualized as being formed from their respective seed-syllables.
Again, visualize yourself in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven of the Form Realm.
One should then perform the mudrā of invitation.
To summon [the deities], snap the fingers; one should thus invite all the Buddhas.
In a single instant, all Buddhas, together with the Vajra Bodhisattvas,
fill all the maṇḍalas; they gather in the assembly maṇḍala as the swift Great Seal— behold Vajrasattva!
By reciting "One Hundred and Eight" once, through the seal of the assembly,
all Tathāgatas become firm; one becomes the Vajrasattva himself,
abiding as a compassionate friend at every gate and in all places.
Performing the activities with the hook and so forth, the mantra for summoning by means of the Great Karma-mudrā is as follows:
Next, one should form the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); with both hands, form the vajra-fists.
Interlace the wrists and bind the *dhī* and *prajñā* fingers;
the index fingers should be like a great hook, like a rope, and also like a chain, with the backs of the hands pressed together.
The mantra of the Vajrāṅkuśa is as follows:
The mantra of Vajrāṅkuśī (Vajra Hook) is: VAJRA AṄKUŚI HŪṂ.
The mantra of Vajrapāśī (Vajra Lasso) is: VAJRA PĀŚI HŪṂ. The mantra of Vajrasphoṭā (Vajra Chain) is: [VAJRA SPHOṬA HŪṂ].
VAJRAŚAṄKARI ĀḤ. The mantra of the vajra bell is as follows:
"By means of the vajra hook, one is able to summon;
by means of the ritual of the vajra noose, one is able to draw in all."
Through the application of the Vajra-Chain, one is capable of all fetters;
by being bound through the Vajra-entry, one is able to accomplish all pūrvasevās.
Then, one holds the arghya vessel.
Recite the hundred-syllable mantra and offer it:
Oṃ vajrasattva samayam anupālaya vajrasattva-tvenopatiṣṭha.
4. *saṃkrodha-stambhana* 5. *nirdhūta-māravam* 6.

VAṂ SVĀTĪTAGATA VAJRAMAṆI MUNCA VĀRIPĀVA MAHASAMAYASATTVA ĀH.
This is the hundred-syllable mantra.
Because one offers *argha* water,
all prayers and aspirations shall be swiftly accomplished.
Next, recite the Vajralāsyā mantra as follows:
Hrīḥ vajra-vilāsini traṭ. Next, the mantra of Vajramālā is:
Hrīḥ vajra he he ha ha. Next, the mantra of Vajragīta is:
*Kṣitidhara-vajra* (1) *nidhi nidhi nidhi*. Next, the mantra for the Vajra Dance is:
*Kṣitidhara-vajra* (1) *nṛtye* (2) *vepa vepa* (3). Then, perform the outer offerings once more and present them as an offering.
Next, the mantra of the Vajra Garland is:
Oṃ vajrarati svāhā. The mantra of the Great Vajra Incense is:
Mahārata-vajri svāhā. The mantra of the Vajra Lamp is: [Oṃ vajradīpa svāhā].
Oṃ vajra-gandhe hīḥ. This is the mantra for the Vajra Perfume.
As soon as the practitioner abides in this Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Eight Offerings, [the deities appear].
One is then able to produce vast ocean-like clouds of offering rituals for all Buddha-fields throughout the entirety of the ten directions.
Next, one should bind the samaya-mudrā of the Honored One.
Join the two hands in the vajra-pañjali mudrā;
with each thumb, press against the side of the index finger, and recite the mantra of the deity seven times.
The mantra is as follows:
*Namo bhagavatyai prajñāpāramitāyai | Oṃ hrīḥ jñānaśrī jvala tejovatyai svāhā.* Having recited this mantra, perform the mudrā of scattering upon the crown of the head.
Next, one should recite the mantra for the rosary, which is:
Oṃ vajra-hūṃ-hī-ja-pa-samaye hūṃ. By reciting this mantra seven times over the rosary, it is consecrated.
Reciting it once shall become ten thousand times.
Having thus completed the consecration,
[perform it] four times, three times, or even twice a day.
Recite either one hundred and eight times or one thousand times.
At all times, the number of recitations must remain constant.
When the count for the session is complete, wear [the mantra] upon the crown of the head as before.
He immediately enters the samādhi of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, within his heart, he visualizes a full moon disc whose extent pervades the entire dharma-realm,
and therein he contemplates the letter-gateway *bhū*.
When one dwells with focused attention, clearly and distinctly perceiving form as being like white jade or snow,
this is called *śamatha*.
Once the mind has been gathered from its various distractions and stabilized, it is thus established.
This is then conjoined with wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because one contemplates the meaning of the syllable *bhū*— that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are as the *dharmadhātu* and are unapprehendable—
it is termed *vipaśyanā*.
It is either associated with concentration or associated with wisdom;
having long since become thoroughly proficient, concentration and wisdom are practiced in tandem,
such that the subject of observation and the object of observation are perfectly equal.
One should completely distance oneself from both the grasper and the grasped.
Constantly performing such contemplative observation,
one will enter the first stage (bhūmi) in this very life.
After sixteen great kalpas, one becomes Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Again, bind the mudrā of the principal deity and recite the hundred-syllable mantra.
Re-bind the mudrās of the eight offerings and hold up the argha water.
Gaze to the left with the Vajra-eye to dissolve the boundary.
Then, forming the Dharma-pāramitā mudrā, offer farewell to the noble assembly and recite the Vajra-vimukti mantra:
Oṃ kṛtvaḥ sarvasattvarātasiddhārthata yathānugaccha gaccha bhaṃ buddhavaiśyane punarāgama mānayatu oṃ vajragātra sattvam muḥ. Furthermore, [use] the Vajraratna mudrā.
Having performed the empowerment, donned the armor, and prostrated to the Buddhas of the five directions,
one should immediately leave the maṇḍala and practice walking meditation as desired while reciting Mahāyāna sūtras.
Dedicate these sublime merits toward all sentient beings.
One shall swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Following this, the efficacy [of the mantra] is described as being exceedingly sublime.
The root mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā is as follows:
*Namo bhagavate prajñāpāramitāye | Oṃ hrīḥ jñānaśrī-jayavijaye svāhā.* The Buddha said: "This dhāraṇī-mudrā has four names."
First is named the Inexhaustible Treasury of Prajñā;
second is named the Eye of Prajñā;
third is named the Root of Prajñā.
It is called the Heart of the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā.
This dhāraṇī-seal possesses great merit;
if one can receive and uphold it with a sincere mind according to the Dharma, [great benefits will follow].
With each recitation, eighteen thousand *sūtra* treasuries are produced;
furthermore, from within each of those individual *sūtras*,
twenty-five thousand *sūtra* treasuries are respectively produced.
Furthermore, from within each and every sūtra,
ten million sūtra-piṭakas are produced;
and from within each and every sūtra-piṭaka, [ten million further piṭakas are produced].
Therein are produced immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of sūtra-piṭakas;
thus, through successive transmission,
there arise immeasurable and inexhaustible sūtra-piṭakas.
The titles, phrases, names, meanings,
and flavors of the sūtras produced are each distinct and do not repeat;
thus, they are born forth inexhaustibly from moment to moment.
Therefore, it is called the Seal of the Dhāraṇī of the Inexhaustible Treasury.
This dhāraṇī seal is the ancestral source of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
It is also the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time,
the mother of all *prajñāpāramitā*,
and that which has been constantly offered to, revered, and praised by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future.
If good sons or good daughters, with a sincere heart,
copy, read, recite, and practice according to the teaching,
all their heavy sins of birth and death throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges-sand eons [shall be extinguished].
In a mere moment, all [obstacles] are extinguished without remainder.
As for the merits of this dhāraṇī-seal,
were I to remain for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, [I could not fully describe them].
Even [the Buddha] could not exhaustively praise it;
how much less could any other person praise it to the end?
If one wishes to practice the Dharma of Prajñā, [one should do so].
Having fasted for one meal, bathed in fragrant water while observing the precepts, and donned new, clean robes, enter the *maṇḍala*.
One must first recite this *dhāraṇī* and form this mudrā one million times; thereafter, when practicing other *prajñā* methods, they will certainly achieve accomplishment.
Therefore, it is called the root of Prajñā.
This dhāraṇī-seal is fully capable of illuminating all dharmas of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore, it is called the Eye of Prajñāpāramitā.
This dhāraṇī-seal is fully capable of destroying all obstacles.
It is called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya* because it is fully capable of upholding all the merits of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
One scroll of the ritual for the cultivation of the Bodhisattva’s contemplative practice and recitation of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
